cues.text: The binomial theorem connects multiplication with combinations.
For a positive integer n, the expression a plus b raised to n is a product of
n
identical factors.
To produce a term containing r copies of b, choose b from exactly r factors
and
a from all the others.
There are C of n, r ways to choose those factors.
Each contributes a to the power n minus r times b to the power r.
Adding over r from zero through n gives the finite expansion.
There are n plus one indexed terms, with the first using no b and the last
using only b.
For n equal to four, the coefficients are one, four, six, four, one.
Every term has total degree four in a and b.
The symmetry of the coefficients follows by exchanging the selected and
unselected factors.
This counting proof explains why combinations appear instead of permutations:
the selected factor positions form a subset.
The finite formula applies to positive integer exponents in this class.
An exponent such as one half does not produce the same finite expansion.
If specific substitutions make some terms vanish or combine, distinguish that
simplified expression from the original indexed binomial list.
The general term is indexed by r, but its position in the expansion is r plus
one.
The first term uses r equal to zero, so the third term uses r equal to two.
This distinction prevents many off by one errors.
To find the coefficient of x cubed in two x minus three raised to five, take a
as two x and b as negative three.
The general term is C of five, r times two x to the power five minus r times
negative three to the power r.
The variable power is five minus r, so matching it to three gives r equal to
two.
The coefficient is C of five, two times two cubed times negative three
squared,
or ten times eight times nine, giving seven hundred twenty.
The full term is seven hundred twenty x cubed; the coefficient alone is seven
hundred twenty.
For the x to the fourth term, r equals one, so its coefficient is five times
sixteen times negative three, or negative two hundred forty.
Bracket the negative base before taking a power.
Finally, check that the solved r is an integer in the allowed range from zero
to five before evaluating the combination.
A binomial may contain the variable in both of its parts.
For x squared plus one over x raised to six, the denominator requires x
nonzero.
The general term is C of six, r times x squared to the power six minus r times
one over x to the power r.
Combine the exponents to obtain x to the power twelve minus three r.
For a constant term, set that exponent to zero, giving r equal to four.
The coefficient is C of six, four, or fifteen.
The term occupies position five because the term number is r plus one.
To find the x cubed term instead, solve twelve minus three r equals three,
giving r equal to three and coefficient twenty.
Do not assume that every requested power occurs.
If the outer exponent were five, the variable exponent would be ten minus
three
r.
Setting it to zero would require r equal to ten thirds, which is not an
integer.
Therefore that expansion has no constant term.
The finite binomial theorem still applies even though the resulting expression
contains negative powers of x.
Retain the original nonzero domain condition while simplifying all terms.
The number of terms, not the exponent by itself, determines how many middle
terms exist.
An exponent n gives n plus one indexed terms.
When n is even, that count is odd and there is one central term at position n
divided by two plus one.
Thus a plus b raised to eight has nine terms, and its middle is the fifth
term.
It uses r equal to four and is seventy a to the fourth b to the fourth.
When n is odd, the term count is even and there are two central positions.
For exponent seven there are eight terms, so take positions four and five,
corresponding to r equal to three and four.
In one plus two x raised to seven, the fourth term is C of seven, three times
two x cubed, giving two hundred eighty x cubed.
The fifth is C of seven, four times two x to the fourth, giving five hundred
sixty x to the fourth.
Their binomial coefficients are equal, but the complete terms need not have
equal numerical coefficients after substitution.
Write the term positions first, convert them to r values, and then substitute
into the general term.
This keeps term indexing separate from any special form of a or b.
Suppose a polynomial F of x is written as the sum of coefficients c r times
x to the power r.
Substituting x equal to one makes every variable power equal to one, so F of
one is the sum of all coefficients.
Substituting negative one gives the sum of even power coefficients minus the
sum of odd power coefficients.
For one plus x raised to a positive integer n, these values are two to the
power n and zero.
Adding and subtracting the two equations shows that the even and odd
coefficient sums are each two to the power n minus one.
For n equal to six, the total sum is sixty four and each parity sum is thirty
two.
The positive exponent condition matters: for n equal to zero there is only the
constant coefficient, so the parity sums are not equal.
The same evaluation technique applies to other polynomials, but the numerical
results change.
For two minus three x raised to four, the sum of coefficients is its value at
one, namely one.
Its alternating coefficient sum is the value at negative one, namely six
hundred twenty five.
Keep the polynomial and the chosen evaluation point visible rather than
memorizing two to the n for every binomial.
A weighted coefficient sum can be understood by counting marked subsets.
Take n distinct objects and count pairs consisting of a subset and one marked
member of that subset.
If the subset has size r, it contributes r choices for the mark, so the total
is the sum of r times C of n, r.
Alternatively, choose the marked object first in n ways.
Each of the other n minus one objects may be included or excluded
independently.
The count is n times two to the power n minus one.
For an ordered pair of distinct marked members, the same argument gives n
times
n minus one times two to the power n minus two, provided n is at least two.
Counting by subset size instead gives the sum of r times r minus one times C
of
n, r.
For n equal to five, the first weighted sum is eighty and the ordered pair sum
is one hundred sixty.
Since r squared equals r times r minus one plus r, the sum of r squared times
C
of five, r is two hundred forty.
The ordered nature of the two marks matters; using an unordered pair would
introduce an additional factor of one half.
State what is marked before choosing a weighted identity.
Neighbouring binomial coefficients can be compared without calculating every
factorial.
The ratio of C of n, r plus one to C of n, r is n minus r divided by r plus
one.
As r increases, this ratio moves from above one to below one.
This explains the central greatest coefficient or equal central pair.
For exponent five, the coefficient row is one, five, ten, ten, five, one; its
greatest coefficients are the two tens.
Complete numerical terms can have different maxima because their powers also
contribute.
In one plus two raised to five, the indexed terms are C of five, r times two
to
the power r.
The ratio of the next term to the current term is two times five minus r
divided by r plus one.
The numerical list is one, ten, forty, eighty, eighty, thirty two.
Its greatest terms are the fourth and fifth, each eighty.
The equality case in the ratio must be retained to find both.
This argument compares positive terms; for signed expressions distinguish
algebraically greatest values from greatest magnitudes.
If a variable appears, its specified value and sign are needed before ranking
complete terms.
A greatest coefficient question and a greatest numerical term question
therefore require different comparisons.
A product coefficient receives contributions from every pair of powers that
adds to the requested exponent.
For one plus x raised to four times one plus x raised to five, the product is
one plus x raised to nine.
Its x cubed coefficient is therefore C of nine, three, or eighty four.
Expanding the factors separately gives the same result by summing C of four, r
times C of five, three minus r over the valid indices.
This is a finite coefficient identity, often called Vandermonde's identity.
Its reason is the same selection count split between two disjoint groups.
For factors with different weights or signs, do not combine their exponents as
though their bases were identical.
Consider the product of two binomial powers: one plus two x, all cubed,
multiplied by one minus x, all squared.
The x squared coefficient has three contributions: twelve from x squared times
the constant, negative twelve from the two x coefficients, and one from the
constant times x squared.
Their sum is one.
Write each contribution explicitly to preserve signs.
For coefficient extraction, only terms up to the desired degree are needed,
which can save substantial expansion work.
A coefficient condition can determine an unknown exponent or parameter.
If the coefficient of x squared in one plus x raised to n is forty five, then
C
of n, two equals forty five.
This gives n times n minus one equals ninety, or n squared minus n minus
ninety
equals zero.
Factoring yields n equal to ten or negative nine.
The stated exponent is a positive integer, so only ten is admissible.
If the ratio C of n, three divided by C of n, two equals two,
simplifying gives n minus two divided by three equals two, hence n equal to
eight.
This ratio presumes the relevant coefficients exist and the denominator is
nonzero.
Now let the coefficient of x squared in one plus a x raised to four be twenty
four.
That coefficient is six a squared, so a squared equals four.
For real a there are two possibilities, plus two and minus two.
A positive answer cannot be chosen without another condition.
If the coefficient of x is additionally eight, then four a equals eight and
selects a equal to two.
Solve the algebra, then restore all original integer, domain and sign
restrictions.
A finite expansion is exact when every term is retained.
Approximating means deliberately discarding some of those terms.
For one plus t raised to five, the exact coefficients are one, five, ten, ten,
five, one.
With t equal to zero point zero two, retaining only the constant and linear
term gives one point one zero.
Retaining the quadratic term as well gives one point one zero four.
The exact value is one point one zero four zero eight zero eight zero three
two.
Because t is positive, all omitted terms here are positive, so both
truncations
underestimate the exact value.
The error after the quadratic term is ten t cubed plus five t to the fourth
plus t to the fifth.
For zero at most t at most zero point zero two, replacing t in each positive
remainder term by zero point zero two bounds that error by eight point zero
eight zero three two times ten to the power negative five.
Check a requested accuracy before deciding how many terms to keep.
A different application uses integer divisibility: write five to the fifth as
one plus four raised to five.
Modulo sixteen, every term from r equal to two onward is divisible by sixteen.
The remainder is therefore that of one plus twenty, namely five.
These applications use the same exact positive integer expansion with clearly
stated operations.
